market.note: D06 revision. (1) unitsPerSlotMonth stays 6,000 (200 orders a day): still a planning point, not a statistic. Cross-checks found: Joe Coffee, an ordering app for independent shops, reports an average ticket of $8.47 across its shops (was $7.82 a year earlier; its method is not stated), which matches the pack's $8.50; BizBuySell's median coffee shop sold in the US takes $375,000 a year = $1,027 a day = about 121 orders a day at that ticket, so 200 a day is a good New York block, not the national middle. (2) priceElasticity stays -1.3 and now has an anchor: Starbucks North America, second quarter of fiscal 2025, transactions fell 4% while prices rose about 3% (-4 / 3 = -1.3). Range: -1.0 (USDA ERS report ERR-139, Okrent and Alston: own-price elasticity of all food away from home -1.02, limited service less elastic than full service) to -2.5 (Starbucks US, fourth quarter of fiscal 2024: ticket +4%, transactions -10%, a quarter with other troubles mixed in). (3) weights: reputation cut from 0.20 to 0.09, the other three keep their old ratios to each other (35 : 25 : 20). Reason: Luca (Harvard Business School working paper 12-016) measured +5-9% revenue per Yelp star for independent restaurants. In the engine one star = 0.25 of the 0-1 reputation scale, and the demand change is |elasticity| x (reputation weight / price weight) x 0.25 x (1 - own share). Old weights: 1.3 x (0.20 / 0.35) x 0.25 x 0.9 = 16.7% per star, twice the top of the measured range. New weights: 1.3 x (0.09 / 0.40) x 0.25 x 0.9 = 6.6% per star. The letter grade and word of mouth act on top of this through events and mechanics (extra.mechanics: star_rating, letter_grade_demand). Toast's 2025 survey of 650 US coffee drinkers supports keeping quality close to price: taste 53%, price 20%, convenience 17%, atmosphere 8% as the main reason to pick one shop over another (stated, not measured). All numbers were read in search results; the pages themselves could not be opened from this session.

extra.d06HowNumbersWereChecked: This session could run web searches but could not open pages: the environment's network policy blocked direct requests to every site tried (www.nyc.gov, square.com, www.placer.ai). So nothing in this fragment is marked verified. Every number carries the page it was reported from and an 'evidence' tag: primary_via_search (the search tool quoted it from the primary page: a city or state agency, a company's own filing or price page, a statute), study_via_search (a published study, quoted from its abstract or the authors' pages), industry_via_search (a company's report on its own customers, a trade publication or a news report), anecdote (owners' words), assumption (my arithmetic or a planning value; the note shows it). A reader with network access should open the 'source' and upgrade primary_via_search items to verified.
extra.weekdayMultNote: Mon..Sun; sums to 7. D06 revision for a neighborhood cafe (the East Village map). Anchors: Toast, cafes and bakeries on its platform, April-June 2023: Saturday +15% and Friday +9% transactions against the weekly average; Monday is the slowest day, about 10% under the average. The other four days share what is left (3.86) by my estimate: Tuesday to Thursday rising toward the weekend, Sunday just under average. The old profile (1, 1, 1, 1, 1.05, 1.05, 0.9) had Sunday as the weakest day and no Monday dip, which is the pattern of an office district, not of a residential one. Use extra.weekdayProfiles for other kinds of block. Numbers read in search results; pages not opened.

weekdayProfiles.note: Four week shapes, each Mon..Sun and summing to 7, so the weekly total stays what the engine computes and only its split changes. Pick by what stands near the door (place.anchors from city data). All are estimates built from the measurements listed; none is a measured cafe series for New York.

neighborhood.use: Residential blocks: East Village, Park Slope, Astoria
neighborhood.basis: Toast cafe and bakery data 2023: Saturday +15%, Friday +9%, Monday -10% against the weekly average

office.use: Office districts: Midtown, Financial District, Downtown Brooklyn
office.basis: Placer.ai share of weekday office visits, January-October 2025, US: Tuesday 24.3%, Wednesday 23.7%, Thursday 21.8%, Friday 12.4%, so Monday 17.8%; New York's Friday share in the first half of 2026 was 11.9%. I assume 70% of an office-district cafe's weekday orders follow office attendance and 30% do not, Saturday at 35% and Sunday at 25% of an average weekday, then scale to 7. Raw: 0.92, 1.15, 1.13, 1.06, 0.73, 0.35, 0.25.

transit.use: Next to a busy subway entrance
transit.basis: MTA, October 2026: Tuesday-Thursday above 4.4 million rides, record Thursday 4.72 million, record Friday 4.51 million, record Saturday 3.59 million, record Sunday 3.14 million; Streetsblog: Mondays about 7% under Tuesday-Friday. Ordinary weekend days are well under the records, so Saturday 0.70 and Sunday 0.55 of midweek are my estimates.

tourist.use: Tourist corridors: SoHo, Times Square edge, Brooklyn Bridge Park
tourist.basis: My estimate: weekend-heavy. No day-of-week series for visitor spending was found.

hourCurve.note: Share of a day's orders by clock hour, 24 numbers each summing to 1 (index 0 = midnight to 1am). The engine has no hours yet; this is the input for extra.mechanics hourly_peak. The shapes are drawn by hand and checked against four measurements. Placer.ai 2024, share of visits between 6:00 and 9:59am: Dunkin' 39.9%, Starbucks 29.9%; between 3:00 and 6:59pm: Starbucks 23.7%, Dunkin' 16.4%. Starbucks (Wall Street Journal, February 2026): more than half of US company-store sales happen before 11am. A convenience-store operator in NACS Magazine: 6-10am is more than half of coffee sales. Cafe consultants put the 7-9am rush at 35-45% of the day (one Square merchant: 42% in two hours). The neighborhood curve (a Starbucks-like, lingering shop) has 46% of orders before 11am and 23% from 3 to 7pm; the office curve (a Dunkin'-like commuter shop) has 53% before 11am and 16% from 3 to 7pm.

monthCurve.note: Demand by calendar month for a New York neighborhood cafe, Jan..Dec, per day (game months have 30 days), averaging 1 and summing to 12. My estimate; no monthly sales series for New York cafes was found. What it leans on: (a) Census Monthly Retail Trade, food services and drinking places, not seasonally adjusted, 2025, $ million: August 104,429; September 97,102; October 100,802; November 96,332; December 99,612 (read on FRED, series MRTSSM722USN; January-July 2025 were not shown in the search results); (b) Placer.ai office index: visits slump from late July to Labor Day and again, harder, from Thanksgiving through the first weeks of January (July 2025: 21.8% under 2019; December 2025: 33.1% under 2019); (c) trade press: cafe customers 'disappear at the beginning of every year' (Fresh Cup); (d) autumn drink launches lift coffee visits (Placer.ai: Starbucks +3.4% in October and +14.7% in November 2021 month over month). New York differs from the national series in August: residents leave and offices thin out, so August is below average here although it is the national peak.
realSignals: Census Monthly Retail Trade, food services and drinking places, not seasonally adjusted (FRED MRTSSM722USN, MRTSSM7222USN)
Placer.ai monthly office index; Kastle weekly occupancy
CoStar monthly hotel occupancy for New York City (May 2025 87.9%, September 86.6%, October 89.4%)

guestSegments.note: Who buys, by kind of block. Shares of orders are my estimates: nobody publishes this split, and every guide says the same thing, count the people yourself at 8am, 1pm and 5pm on a weekday and on a Saturday. The sizes of the groups are real: see 'facts'. The engine treats all customers as one crowd; extra.mechanics guest_segments describes the split.

channels.note: Where an order comes from and what is left of each dollar. Contribution = 1 - cost of goods 28% - what the channel takes; labor and rent are not in it. In-store card costs are the pack's own (2.55% + $0.135 an order = 4.1% of an $8.50 ticket). Shares are planning ranges, not statistics for New York cafes.

list.name: Counter: stay or take away
list.basis: The pack's reference point. National Restaurant Association with Circana: 83% of limited-service traffic was off-premises in 2024 (76% in 2019), drive-thrus included

list.name: Order-ahead on your own page
list.basis: Square Online free plan: 3.3% + 30 cents an online order = 6.8% of $8.50. Starbucks: mobile orders are 33% of US company-store transactions (third quarter of fiscal 2026); Dutch Bros: 11.5% in mid-2025, about 14% by year end. Independents sit lower

list.name: Pickup ordered in a delivery app
list.basis: DoorDash pickup commission 6% on every plan plus card processing about 3%

list.name: Delivery app, basic listing
list.basis: New York City caps: 15% delivery + 5% basic service + 3% card processing. Limited-service delivery was 9% of traffic in 2024 (4% in 2019); a cafe's small tickets put it under that

list.name: Delivery app with marketing services
list.basis: Since Local Law 79 of 2025 an app may add up to 20% for optional enhanced services if it also offers the basic plan: 15 + 5 + 3 + 20 = 43%. DoorDash's national plans are 15%, 25% and 30% delivery commission

list.name: Office catering through a marketplace
list.basis: ezCater: 15% of food and delivery fee + 2.99% payment fee; 7% when the order comes through your own page; its own drivers cost 10% of the food total, $30 minimum

list.name: Prepaid pass or subscription
list.basis: Margin depends on how often holders come. Panera: $14.99 a month, capped at 30 drinks a month from August 19, 2026 after years as 'unlimited'

queue.note: What limits a rush and when people leave. Service times are trade figures; the walk-away curve is my estimate tied to two measurements: people judge a line by its length, and patience for a coffee is about six minutes.

basis.what: One barista on a two-group machine makes about 30 drinks an hour, two together about 60; 50 is 'the more truthful figure' for a two-group machine, 100 the ceiling
About one minute for an espresso and two for a milk drink
Starbucks target since August 2025: four minutes in the cafe and drive-thru, twelve for mobile and delivery; about half of orders met four minutes before

Lu, Musalem, Olivares and Schilkrut, Management Science 59(8), 2013, a supermarket deli counter: customers react to the length of the queue, not to how fast it moves; a moderate rise in the number of people in line cuts sales like a 5% price increase; the effect is significant above about five people
UK survey of 5,000 consumers, 2014: people wait 6 minutes 2 seconds on average for a coffee before leaving
Waitwhile 2023: ten minutes is the longest acceptable wait for food and drink
Starbucks, first quarter of fiscal 2017: 1,200 stores took 20% or more of peak orders by mobile (13 a year before); the crowd at the handoff made walk-in customers leave without ordering

ratingModel.note: How reviews and the window grade move sales. Effects are from published studies; the mapping to the engine's 0-1 reputation is mine: 4.25 stars = 0.5 (the average US cafe profile is rated 4.26), one star = 0.25.

revenuePerStar.appliesTo: independents only; chains show no effect

halfStarStep.what: Yelp rounds to half stars: 3.74 shows as 3.5, 3.76 as 4. The extra half star made restaurants sell out 19 percentage points (49%) more often

replyingToReviews.what: Hotels that began answering reviews gained 0.12 stars; a third of them moved up half a star on the display within six months (Proserpio and Zervas, Marketing Science 36(5), 2017)

yelpFilter.what: Yelp says about three quarters of reviews are 'recommended'; the rest do not count toward the stars, and reviews the business asked for are filtered more often

letterGrade.what: 88% of New Yorkers said they considered the letter grade when choosing where to eat (2012 survey, Wong and others, American Journal of Public Health 105(3), 2015). Rothbart, Schwartz and others, Public Administration Review 79, 2019, 28 months of sales-tax data on more than 15,000 restaurants: an A raises revenue and lowers the chance of closing relative to a B; a C lowers revenue and raises the chance of closing relative to a B. The sizes were not shown in what I could read, so the multipliers below are my planning values.

onlineToo.what: The grade is not only in the window: Yelp has shown New York City inspection results on restaurant pages since 2013 and health scores nationwide since 2018, under the price range, with the list of violations one click away. The city's own lookup shows them too

typicalRatings.what: A 2026 benchmark of 500 cafe and 570 restaurant profiles by a review-software company; it describes its sample, not the industry. An older BrightLocal study put all local businesses at 4.42 on average

competition.note: What is around the door in New York and what it does. Counts are from news reports of the Center for an Urban Future's yearly chain census; the size of the hit from a new rival is not measured anywhere I could find, so the ranges are planning values.

chainCounts.note: The largest chain in the city; passed Starbucks in Manhattan for the first time
Closed 42 New York stores in 2025, the most of any chain that stayed

First two US stores opened in June 2025 in Greenwich Village and Chelsea with $1.99 opening drinks; app and kiosk ordering; has taken former Starbucks sites; the date of the 22-store count was not confirmed
Worldwide count; about 500 sq ft a store, automatic espresso machines, two or three staff; matcha is about half of sales

effectOfANewRivalWithin250m.basis: Marketing Science 2018 (Starbucks closures): one more Starbucks within a mile takes 1.2% of a Starbucks store's sales, 0.4% at one to three miles: small, and between identical stores. Owners' accounts run both ways: one Hanover, New Hampshire cafe reported falling sales after a Starbucks opened; in Minneapolis one neighbor lost coffee sales and another lost none. NBER working paper 32604: a new Starbucks changes nothing measurable in tracts that already had cafes.

streetCarts.note: Intro 431, enacted over a veto in January 2026: 2,200 more mobile food vendor supervisory license applications each year through 2031. A coffee cart at the subway stairs sells the commuter's drip coffee for about half a cafe's price.

demandEvidence.note: Every demand number the engine or the keen-cray branch assumes, against what could be found. status: confirmed (evidence supports the value), corrected (this fragment changes it), range_only (evidence gives a range, the value is inside or outside it as noted), not_found.

rows.basis: Joe Coffee (an ordering app for independents; method not stated): $8.47 across its shops, $7.82 a year earlier. Toast medians: drip coffee $3.65 (February 2026, +4.3% in a year), cold brew $5.75 (October 2026, +4.0%), latte $5.46 (early 2024); New York lattes are quoted at $6.00-$7.50
Median sold US coffee shop: $375,000 a year = 121 orders a day at $8.47. The research notes' New York break-even runs 159-267 a day by rent tier

rows.unit: percent of orders per percent of price

rows.basis: A site-selection guide's rule: coffee and lunch places convert 2-4% of passers-by (fast food 3-5%, casual dining 1-3%). 0.088 is the rate with no rival in sight; with the rivals of a typical East Village block the branch's formula lands near 4-5%, the top of the rule. No measurement for New York was found

10.6 is the average over a whole shift with cleaning, stocking and slow hours. At the bar in a rush one barista makes about 30 drinks = 25 orders an hour. The daily average is right; the missing piece is the hour: see extra.mechanics hourly_peak

rows.where: engine: SPILL = 0.5 of turned-away buyers try a neighbor
rows.basis: No measurement of where a person who leaves a coffee line goes. What is measured: patience about six minutes; people judge the line by its length. See extra.queue

rows.unit: demand multiplier with a B in the window
rows.basis: Direction measured (A above B above C in revenue and survival), size not seen. The city's own 2012 figure, restaurant sales up 9.3% in the nine months after grading began, is a before-and-after comparison; the controlled studies found no gain for the average restaurant

rows.unit: change in orders when a rival opens within 250 m

rows.basis: No measured opening curve. Owners four months in still ask on forums when numbers settle; blogs give 6-18 months to break even, 18-30 in crowded cities; one cafe's own figure: 20-70% of first-time customers do not return within 100 days. Chains: Placer.ai notes that a new location in an unfamiliar market traditionally settles at about 75% of an established market's visits after an opening 'honeymoon', and that recent openings run below that

rows.unit: share of revenue from repeat customers
rows.basis: Square case study 65-70%; a general small-business estimate 25-40%; RestoLabs: 38.2% of cafe customers come back within six months
Delivery was 9% of limited-service traffic in 2024, 4% in 2019. New York apps carried 3.3 million orders a week in mid-2026, 700,000 more than in December 2023

eventCatalog.realFrequency: Not found

eventCatalog.name: Your rating slips under four stars
eventCatalog.text: On the map you are now the 3.9 between two 4.4s. Newcomers and tourists pick by that number.
eventCatalog.trigger: The shop's star rating (extra.mechanics star_rating) falls below 4.0
eventCatalog.realSignal: The rating shown on Google Maps and Yelp
eventCatalog.realFrequency: BrightLocal 2026: 68% of consumers want at least four stars before using a local business; 31% want four and a half, up from 17% a year earlier. In a 2026 sample of 570 restaurant profiles 14.9% were rated under 4.0 and the average was 4.27; 500 US cafe profiles averaged 4.26
eventCatalog.note: A threshold on top of the smooth star effect: the people who filter by four stars never see the shop. Regulars do not care, so the hit is on newcomers only: 5% of all orders is my estimate for a shop where about a third of orders come from people who do not know it yet.

eventCatalog.name: The rating rounds up half a star
eventCatalog.text: Your average crept from 4.2 to 4.3 and the site now shows four and a half stars. Nothing else changed.
eventCatalog.trigger: The average rating crosses a rounding line (x.25 or x.75) upward
eventCatalog.realSignal: The displayed, rounded rating on Yelp
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Anderson and Magruder, 2012: restaurants just above a rounding line sold out 19 percentage points (49%) more often than those just below
eventCatalog.note: Half of Luca's 5-9% per star is 2.5-4.5%; 4% is used. The same step down costs the same.

eventCatalog.name: The reviews start saying 'slow'
eventCatalog.text: For a month the morning line moved slower than people's patience. Now the newest reviews all mention the wait.
eventCatalog.trigger: More than 5% of a month's demand was lost for lack of staff or bar capacity
eventCatalog.realSignal: Share of the shop's recent reviews that mention waiting
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Starbucks' own count before its 2025 turnaround: only about half of orders were ready within four minutes
eventCatalog.note: The size is my estimate: a quarter of a star (0.06 on the reputation scale) for a month of visible waits. BrightLocal's 2026 survey stresses that recent reviews decide.

eventCatalog.name: Phone orders pile up at the handoff
eventCatalog.text: Twenty cups with stickers crowd the counter at 8:15. People in line watch them being made first, and some leave.
eventCatalog.trigger: Order-ahead runs with no cap while the rush hour is above 85% of bar capacity
eventCatalog.realSignal: Share of rush-hour orders placed ahead; Starbucks counted stores above 20%
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Starbucks, early 2017: 1,200 stores took 20% or more of rush orders by phone, up from 13 stores a year before
eventCatalog.note: Starbucks' chief operating officer named the congestion at the handoff as the biggest cause of a weak quarter: people saw the crowd and did not order. Sizes are my estimates. In 2025 the company answered with a queueing algorithm and capped pickup slots.

eventCatalog.name: A big price jump gets noticed
eventCatalog.text: You raised prices by more than 8% in one go. Regulars do the sum at the register and say so online.
eventCatalog.trigger: The price order rises more than 8% within one month
eventCatalog.realSignal: The shop's own price history against the drift of menu prices (Toast: about 4% a year)
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Toast: the median drip coffee rose 4.3% in the year to February 2026 and the median cold brew 4.0% in the year to October 2026
eventCatalog.note: On top of the ordinary elasticity. Owners in 2025: 'You always get nervous when you raise prices... you may lose some, especially at first' (Indianapolis); in Colorado most customers understood and changed nothing. Trade advice is to move in small steps and say why. 3% for two months is my estimate.

eventCatalog.name: The map says you are open, the door says you are not
eventCatalog.text: You changed your hours and the listing did not. A few people came to a locked door and wrote about it.
eventCatalog.trigger: The hours lever changed while the reviews lever is set to 'ignore'
eventCatalog.realSignal: Hours shown on the shop's map listings against real hours
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Not found. One turnaround story: a cafe's sales recovered within two months once people learned it was still open and it had a web presence
eventCatalog.note: Sizes are my estimates.

eventCatalog.name: A coffee chain opens within sight
eventCatalog.text: A national chain takes the corner unit. It will pull the commuters who only want a fast cup; your regulars are yours to keep.
eventCatalog.realSignal: New food service permits and storefront leases on the block; the chain counts of the Center for an Urban Future
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Dunkin' has 623 stores in the city (2025); Starbucks had 328 in 2024 and closed 42 in 2025; every block within reach of a subway stop already has one or expects one
eventCatalog.note: See events chain_opens_nearby. After six months the effect should fade to about -3%: the people who switched were the least attached.

eventCatalog.name: An app-only chain opens with $1.99 coffee
eventCatalog.text: A new chain two blocks away runs on an app and kiosks and hands every new user a $1.99 drink. Price shoppers will try it.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Store count of app-first chains in the city: 2 in June 2025, 22 by 2026
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Luckin Coffee opened its first two US stores in Greenwich Village and Chelsea in June 2025 with $1.99 opening drinks and had 22 New York stores within about a year, some in former Starbucks sites
eventCatalog.note: 5% for the three months of opening coupons is my estimate; the effect is strongest on students and weakest on regulars.

eventCatalog.name: A 500-square-foot rival opens next door
eventCatalog.text: A venture-backed chain fits a counter, an automatic machine and two staff into a space a third of yours. Its rent per cup is lower than yours.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Small-format chain store counts
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Blank Street: 106 stores worldwide by August 2026 after a $105 million funding round; stores of about 500 sq ft with automatic espresso machines and two or three staff; matcha is about half of its sales
eventCatalog.note: What the rival cannot offer is seats and a reason to stay; the moves listed are the ones that sell that. 5% is my estimate.

eventCatalog.name: The chain store on the block closes
eventCatalog.text: The chain did not renew. A few hundred people a day need a new morning stop.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Chain closures: Starbucks closed 42 New York stores in 2025
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Chains in New York City shrank 1.3% in 2025 (112 stores), the sixth decline in eight years; 18 chains left the city entirely
eventCatalog.note: The gain is real only if the shop can serve it: chain customers expect phone ordering and a four-minute wait. 6% is my estimate.

eventCatalog.name: The cafe across the street closes
eventCatalog.text: Its regulars are loyal to their order, not to the room. Some will try you this week.
eventCatalog.realSignal: A rival's bankruptcy or closure on the same block (in the game: another player or a resident business)
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Follows from the game itself: the engine already hands half of turned-away buyers to neighbors
eventCatalog.note: 4% is my estimate; the engine's own split of the block's passers-by may already produce it, in which case this entry is only the announcement text.

eventCatalog.text: A licensed cart sells drip coffee and a roll for about half your price, exactly where commuters surface.

eventCatalog.realFrequency: 6,880 food vendor permits before the 2026 reform; a waiting list of more than 10,000
eventCatalog.note: See events coffee_cart_at_the_stairs.

eventCatalog.text: From next month the tower around the corner fills on Mondays and Fridays too.

eventCatalog.name: The office building next door is being converted to apartments
eventCatalog.text: The tenants are gone and the scaffolding is up. For a year or two nobody works or lives there; after that, a thousand neighbors.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Department of Buildings conversion filings; the Comptroller's office-to-residential tracker
eventCatalog.realFrequency: More than 15 million sq ft of office conversions under way in New York, about 16,000-17,400 apartments; another 9.5-9.8 million sq ft planned to start in 2026; Midtown has passed the Financial District
eventCatalog.note: 10% during construction is my estimate for a shop that drew a fifth of its orders from that building. When the apartments fill, the week shape turns from 'office' to 'neighborhood' (extra.weekdayProfiles).

eventCatalog.name: A new apartment building opens on the block
eventCatalog.text: Several hundred new neighbors arrive within a few months, and none of them has a coffee habit here yet.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Certificates of occupancy for new residential buildings
eventCatalog.realFrequency: See office_tower_becomes_apartments
eventCatalog.note: 4% is my estimate. New residents choose a regular cafe in their first weeks; the shop that is open on their first Saturday keeps them.

eventCatalog.name: The semester starts
eventCatalog.text: Thousands of students are back and looking for their place for the year.
eventCatalog.realSignal: University calendars: NYU fall classes start September 2, 2026; spring classes January 19, 2027
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Twice a year. CUNY about 247,000 students, NYU about 56,800, Columbia about 35,200
eventCatalog.note: 6% is the place model's in-term effect near a college, an assumption there. Students are the most price-sensitive group and the heaviest users of seats.

eventCatalog.name: Finals week: every seat taken by 10am
eventCatalog.text: Students camp for six hours on one drink. Walk-in customers look at the full room and keep walking.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Exam weeks: NYU December 16-22, 2026
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Twice a year, one to two weeks each
eventCatalog.note: Seat turnover is not an event target yet (requests). Sizes are my estimates: a quarter fewer sit-down orders per seat, slightly more people at the door.

eventCatalog.name: Campus empties for the summer
eventCatalog.text: Classes ended and the dorms cleared out. The block is quiet until September.
eventCatalog.realSignal: University calendars
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Every year, mid-May to early September
eventCatalog.note: 12% is the place model's summer effect near a college (keen-cray branch), an assumption there. See events campus_summer_break for the mixed-block version.

eventCatalog.name: A food creator films your block
eventCatalog.text: A video about 'the best coffee street downtown' passes a million views. Saturday's line goes around the corner, at every cafe on the block.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Views of videos tagged with the neighborhood; map searches for the block
eventCatalog.realFrequency: No rate. Cases: a Williamsburg cafe whose owner's video passed six million views had lines down the block and cut the line off at 3pm; a Manhattan luncheonette had two-to-three-hour waits for months after one video and 'wasn't ready'
eventCatalog.note: Announced to the whole block, so it is not luck for one player. The catch is capacity: a shop that cannot serve the surge loses orders and collects 'slow' reviews (slow_service_reviews). 25% for a month is my estimate; the cases suggest it can be far more.

eventCatalog.name: Everyone is back after Labor Day
eventCatalog.text: Schools open, vacations end and the offices fill in the same week. The strongest stretch of the year begins.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Kastle weekly occupancy; MTA daily ridership (records in September and October 2026)
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Every year. 2026: 4,696,692 subway rides on Wednesday September 23 and 4.72 million on Thursday October 29, the highest since the pandemic; Kastle's New York peak of the year was Tuesday October 27 at 87.3%
eventCatalog.note: 5% is extra.monthCurve's September-October level against the year's average.

eventCatalog.name: Summer Fridays
eventCatalog.text: From late July to Labor Day the offices run half empty, most of all on Fridays.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Placer.ai monthly office index; Kastle weekly occupancy; the Friday share of office visits
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Every year. Fridays hold 11.9% of New York's office visits (first half of 2026) against 12.4% nationally in 2025
eventCatalog.note: 8% is for an office-district block (extra.monthCurve.office July-August against average); the mixed-block version is events summer_friday_slump.

eventCatalog.name: Offices empty out for the holidays
eventCatalog.text: From Thanksgiving week to the first days of January the towers thin out.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Placer.ai December office index: 33.1% under 2019 in December 2025
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Every year: the week of Thanksgiving and the last two weeks of December
eventCatalog.note: 15% over a month is for an office-district block: two near-empty weeks out of four. Tourist corridors gain in the same weeks.

eventCatalog.name: January slump
eventCatalog.text: Resolutions, cold mornings and half-empty offices. Owners say customers disappear at the start of every year.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Census monthly food service sales, not seasonally adjusted; the shop's own January against December
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Every year
eventCatalog.note: See events january_slump.

eventCatalog.name: Autumn drink season
eventCatalog.text: The chains launch their autumn drinks in late August. Customers expect something seasonal from you too.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Chain launch dates; Placer.ai visit counts on launch days
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Every year
eventCatalog.note: Should apply to shops running the seasonal drink; shops without one get 0.99. See events autumn_drink_season.

eventCatalog.name: Holiday cups arrive
eventCatalog.text: Red cups and peppermint everything. The chains' launch day is one of their busiest of the year.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Placer.ai: Starbucks visits 44.5% above average on its November 2025 launch day
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Every year
eventCatalog.note: 2% for an independent with a seasonal drink is my estimate.

eventCatalog.name: National Coffee Day: the chains give coffee away
eventCatalog.text: On September 29 half the chains hand out a free or 25-cent coffee through their apps. For one day your drip coffee competes with free.
eventCatalog.realSignal: The chains' published offers for September 29
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Every year. 2026: Dunkin' free medium coffee with a purchase for app members; Tim Hortons and Circle K free coffee; Peet's a 25-cent drip
eventCatalog.note: One day out of thirty: a 15% dip that day is 0.5% of the month, my estimate.

eventCatalog.name: Peak visitor season
eventCatalog.text: Hotels are close to full. Visitors choose a cafe on the map: the stars and the photos do the selling.
eventCatalog.realSignal: CoStar monthly hotel occupancy for New York City; NYC Tourism visitor counts
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Occupancy 87.9% in May 2025, 86.6% in September, 89.4% in October
eventCatalog.note: 8% is for a tourist corridor; events tourist_high_season carries the mixed-block version.

eventCatalog.name: The tourists are gone
eventCatalog.text: January and February are the quietest weeks of the year for visitors.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Monthly hotel occupancy
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Every year. The January and February occupancy figures were not found in this session
eventCatalog.note: 12% is extra.monthCurve.tourist for January-February against the average month, my estimate; the winter hotel numbers behind it were not seen.

eventCatalog.name: Fewer visitors from abroad
eventCatalog.text: International arrivals fell while domestic trips held. Shops on the tourist streets feel it; side streets do not.
eventCatalog.realSignal: NYC Tourism: international visitors 12.5 million in 2025, down 3.2%
eventCatalog.realFrequency: 2025: total visitors 65 million (+0.7%), international 12.5 million (-3.2%). Forecast for 2026: 66.3 million, international 12.9 million
eventCatalog.note: 2% applies to tourist corridors only; international visitors stay longer and spend more per head than domestic ones.

eventCatalog.name: World Cup summer
eventCatalog.text: World Cup matches across the river. Fans fill the bars that show the games; streets near fan zones are packed or closed.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Match schedule June 11 - July 19, 2026; card transaction volumes
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Once. Restaurant transactions in New York and New Jersey +18.5% in the group stage; venues showing matches +63% sales; one restaurant by the stadium -60% on match days
eventCatalog.note: See events world_cup_summer.

eventCatalog.name: Delivery keeps growing
eventCatalog.text: More app orders every year, even with higher courier pay.
eventCatalog.realSignal: The city's delivery app reports: orders per week
eventCatalog.realFrequency: 3.3 million orders a week in June 2026 against 2.6 million in December 2023
eventCatalog.note: See events delivery_orders_keep_growing.

eventCatalog.name: The city reopens the delivery fee caps
eventCatalog.text: The consumer agency is asking whether the caps on app fees are too high or too low. Whatever it recommends lands on your commission.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Department of Consumer and Worker Protection fee-cap review (required every two years) and its rule notices
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Caps set in 2020, made permanent by Local Law 103 of 2021, loosened by Local Law 79 of 2025 (enhanced services up to 20%); a feedback round ran in April 2026 and a recordkeeping rule was proposed in mid-2026. In April 2026 the city won more than $580,000 in refunds for over 380 restaurants from one app
eventCatalog.note: The direction and size of the next change are unknown; 10% more commission is a placeholder for 'the terms move'. deliveryCommission is not an event target yet (requests).

eventCatalog.name: Customers trade down
eventCatalog.text: Households cut small luxuries first. Quick-service visits are falling and a $7 latte is easy to skip.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Placer.ai quick-service visits year over year; Starbucks comparable transactions; University of Michigan consumer sentiment
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Quick-service visits -1.3% in January-July 2026 and -4.5% in May 2026 year over year; Starbucks US transactions -10% in its fourth fiscal quarter of 2024
eventCatalog.note: See events consumers_trade_down. The consumer sentiment reading for autumn 2026 was not found.

eventCatalog.name: Everyone's prices creep up
eventCatalog.text: Coffee shop prices rise about 4% a year. A shop that never moves its prices gets cheaper against the street every month, and gives away margin.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Toast's median menu prices; Bureau of Labor Statistics index of food away from home
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Median drip coffee $3.65 in February 2026 (+4.3% in a year); median cold brew $5.75 in October 2026 (+4.0%)
eventCatalog.note: fairPrice (the engine's reference price) is not an event target yet (requests). Without it the reference price stays at $8.50 for the whole year while real customers' sense of a fair price moves.

eventCatalog.name: The chain's baristas walk out
eventCatalog.text: Picket lines at the chain's unionized stores. Some of its customers will not cross them and look for coffee nearby.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Strike announcements by the union; list of struck stores
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Starbucks Workers United struck from the company's 'Red Cup Day' in November 2025 with more than 1,000 workers, New York stores among them; the city's mayor-elect joined a picket in December 2025; in August 2026 the union called for a nationwide boycott
eventCatalog.note: Applies within 250 m of a struck store. No measurement of customers moving to independents was found; 3% is my estimate. The same customers ask how you treat your own staff.

eventCatalog.name: The chain's restrooms are now for customers only
eventCatalog.text: The chain down the street stopped letting everyone in. The people it turns away now ask at your counter.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Chain policy announcements
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Starbucks reversed its seven-year open-door policy in January 2025
eventCatalog.note: cleaningCost is not an event target (requests); 15% more cleaning for an open restroom is my estimate. A shop with fewer than 20 seats has no duty to offer one.

eventCatalog.name: Weekends come back faster than weekdays
eventCatalog.text: The city's weekends are almost as busy as before the pandemic; its weekdays are not. Neighborhood shops gain, office-district shops wait.
eventCatalog.realSignal: MTA ridership against 2019: weekdays and weekends separately
eventCatalog.realFrequency: State Comptroller, April 2026: weekend subway ridership was 89% of 2019 in 2025 (80% in 2024); weekday ridership 74% (68% in 2024)
eventCatalog.note: 3% a year on weekend days for residential blocks is my estimate from the 9-point gain in weekend ridership.

eventCatalog.name: More commuters every year
eventCatalog.text: Weekday ridership sets a new post-pandemic record. Shops at the stairs see it first, between 7 and 9.
eventCatalog.realSignal: MTA weekday ridership: 68% of 2019 in 2024, 74% in 2025, record days in autumn 2026
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Thursday October 29, 2026: 4.72 million rides, 9.7% more than the same day a year earlier
eventCatalog.note: 4% a year for blocks with a subway anchor is my estimate: weekday ridership rose 6 points on a base of 68 (+9%), and not every rider is a new customer.

eventCatalog.name: Everyone wants matcha
eventCatalog.text: Green drinks outsell espresso at the newest chains. Customers ask for them by name, mostly in the afternoon.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Menu mix of fast-growing chains; search interest
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Matcha is about half of Blank Street's sales (2026)
eventCatalog.note: Applies to shops with the wide menu or a seasonal drink; 3% is my estimate. Task D04 owns the ingredient cost.

eventCatalog.name: Regulators go after fake reviews
eventCatalog.text: Warning letters went out to companies with suspicious reviews. Platforms purge and label.
eventCatalog.realSignal: FTC enforcement announcements under the review rule
eventCatalog.realFrequency: The rule took effect on October 21, 2024; the first ten warning letters went out in December 2025
eventCatalog.note: The move here is to stop a shortcut: the event raises the chance that an open fake_reviews trail is checked. 30% more checks is a game value.

eventCatalog.name: The city sweeps for hidden fees
eventCatalog.text: Consumer inspectors are checking receipts against posted prices across the neighborhood.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Consumer protection enforcement announcements; the restaurant surcharge rule amended in 2026
eventCatalog.realFrequency: One restaurant in five now adds some extra fee (National Restaurant Association), up from 16% in 2022; the city adopted amendments to its restaurant surcharge rule in March 2026
eventCatalog.note: A game value for the size. The lawful alternative is the card_pricing lever.

eventCatalog.name: The catering marketplace gets a new owner
eventCatalog.text: A delivery giant is buying the site office managers use to order breakfast. More orders may come; the commission may change.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Merger announcements; the marketplace's fee page
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Uber agreed to buy ezCater in October 2026; current fees are 15% + 2.99%
eventCatalog.note: Applies only to shops with the catering lever on. 1% is my estimate.

eventCatalog.name: A chain caps its 'unlimited' coffee pass
eventCatalog.text: After four years the best-known coffee subscription stopped being unlimited: 30 drinks a month. Heavy users were drinking the margin.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Subscription terms of the large chains
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Panera's pass launched in 2022 at $10.99 a month, cost $14.99 by 2026 and was capped at 30 drinks from August 19, 2026
eventCatalog.note: A lesson more than a shock: a pass must have a cap. 1% is my estimate of displaced pass holders looking for another routine.

eventCatalog.name: The chains go after the afternoon
eventCatalog.text: More than half of a big chain's sales happen before 11am, so it now pushes iced, low-caffeine and energy drinks after lunch. The quiet hours are where the next fight is.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Chain menu launches for the afternoon; share of chain visits between 3 and 7pm (Starbucks 23.7%, Dunkin' 16.4% in 2024)
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Starbucks, 2026: digital menu boards that switch to afternoon items; iced fruit drinks grew at double-digit rates; record food sales with the largest gains in the afternoon
eventCatalog.note: 1% of the day is my estimate of what an independent with no afternoon offer gives up; a shop with the wide menu or a seasonal drink should gain the same amount instead. The afternoon hours are where a neighborhood cafe has spare bar capacity.

eventCatalog.name: Reviews vanish from the map listing
eventCatalog.text: A fault at the map platform hides a quarter of everyone's reviews for weeks. Old shops barely notice; a young shop's rating jumps around.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Platform status notices and reports from local-search trackers
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Google confirmed display bugs in February 2025 and October 2025; one business fell from about 600 reviews to 460 and back; reports continued in early 2026, and some reviews never returned
eventCatalog.note: Applies to shops with fewer than about 100 reviews, where losing a quarter changes the displayed average. 2% of reputation for two months is my estimate. The practical advice from the trackers: keep screenshots of the count and rating, and do not ask customers to repost.

mechanics.title: The day has a shape: sales are lost by the hour, not by the month
mechanics.playerDecision: How many people stand at the bar in each part of the day (peak_schedule lever, staff count), whether to cap order-ahead in the rush, how long to stay open.
mechanics.engineMath: Split the day's demand by extra.hourCurve for the block type. For each hour: bar capacity = baristas on the bar x 25 orders an hour (30 drinks an hour / 1.2 drinks an order), times the menu_size capacity effect. Served = min(demand, capacity); the surplus is not simply lost: it stands in line, and extra.queue.walkAwayByPeopleAhead decides how many leave (mechanic queue_walkaway). Monthly totals are the sums. With this the engine's flat rule (1,700 orders per person a month) stops hiding the 8am problem: at 200 orders a day the 8am hour brings 28-36 orders against 25 from one barista, while 3pm brings 14.
fieldsNeeded: staff schedule: people on the bar by daypart (open, rush, midday, afternoon, close)

mechanics.title: People count the line, not the minutes
mechanics.playerDecision: Nothing new to click: it is what punishes a thin bar at 8am. The player's moves are the rush schedule, the menu size, order-ahead with capped slots, and a second register.
mechanics.engineMath: In each hour, people ahead in line = max(0, arrivals - capacity) carried from the previous quarter-hour. Each arriving customer leaves with the probability in extra.queue.walkAwayByPeopleAhead (0 up to three people ahead, 5% at four to five, 15% at six to eight, 30% at nine to twelve, 50% beyond). Office commuters use the next step up of the table: they are on a clock. Those who leave follow the engine's existing rule: half try a neighbor with room. Those who stay but wait more than six minutes feed slow_service_reviews. Phone orders do not see the line, but each one adds a drink to the bar's queue: uncapped, they lengthen the visible wait for walk-ins (handoff_pileup).

mechanics.planningValues: The walk-away table is a planning curve: only its two anchors are measured (about five people in line, about six minutes). The one-step shift for commuters and the half that try a neighbor (the engine's existing rule) have no source.

mechanics.title: A visible star rating, earned review by review
mechanics.playerDecision: How to treat the listings (reviews lever), and whether to take the shortcuts: buy reviews, or reward good ones.
mechanics.engineMath: Keep two numbers per shop: reviewCount and ratingAverage (1-5), shown rounded to half stars. Each month about 1 order in 150 leaves a review (my assumption: 40 a month at 6,000 orders). The month's reviews average: 4.3 base (US cafe profiles average 4.26), +1.5 x (quality - 0.5), -0.6 if the month had slow_service_reviews, -0.4 if a B or C hangs in the window, -0.3 after a price_step_backlash, +0.12 if the owner replies to reviews. ratingAverage moves toward it by reviewsThisMonth / reviewCount, so a new shop's rating swings and an old shop's barely moves. Demand multiplier for people who do not know the shop yet (newcomer share by segment): 1 + 0.07 x (displayed stars - 4.25), and an extra 0.93 while the displayed rating is under 4.0. Regulars ignore the stars. Bought reviews add 10 five-star reviews a month and open the fake_reviews trail; when found, the platform removes them and shows a warning for 90 days (the 90 days are a game value). In the engine's present model the same thing is carried by reputation with weight 0.09 (see market.note).

They are chosen so that a well-run shop sits near 4.5 stars and a month of long waits costs about a quarter of a star.

mechanics.title: The letter in the window sells or repels
mechanics.playerDecision: After a re-inspection that ends in a B or C: post the grade; or post 'Grade Pending' and contest the violations at the city tribunal; or (shortcut) take the card down.
mechanics.engineMath: Compute the letter from the open violation trails with the pack's extra.inspectionPoints (under 14 points A, 14-27 B, 28 or more C). Demand multiplier while the card hangs: A 1.00, Grade Pending 0.98, B 0.95, C 0.88 (extra.ratingModel.letterGrade), applied to newcomers and halved for regulars. Contesting: the shop posts Grade Pending until the hearing (about a month in the game); at the hearing each violation the player has actually fixed is dismissed and the points are recounted; if the score drops under 14 the shop gets its A, otherwise the B or C goes up and the fines stand. Hiding the card: the loss from passers-by stops but about a third of it remains, because the grade also shows on review sites and the city's lookup (the third is a planning value), but the next inspection or a neighbor's complaint adds grade_card_not_posted ($500). The grade is redone at the next cycle: 150-210 days after a B, 90-150 after a C.

mechanics.title: Five kinds of customer, each with its own week, clock and patience
mechanics.playerDecision: No new control: the player reads the mix on the place card before signing the lease and then tunes hours, schedule, laptops, entry price and listings to the people who are actually there.
mechanics.engineMath: Each place gets a block type from its anchors (office within 250 m: office; college within 400 m: campus; museum, plaza or hotel cluster: tourist; otherwise residential) and with it a segment mix (extra.guestSegments.mixByBlock). Daily demand = sum over segments of share x weekday profile x month profile x event multipliers that name the segment. Each segment carries its own seat use (remote workers 1.0, commuters 0.1), ticket, price sensitivity, patience in line and share of newcomers. Effects: an office block earns its week Tuesday to Thursday and nothing on Sunday; a campus block loses 12% in summer; a tourist block lives on the map rating; a residential block lives on regulars, who forgive a line but notice every price change.

mechanics.title: Every channel keeps a different share of the dollar
mechanics.playerDecision: Which channels to open: order-ahead, a basic or promoted delivery listing, catering; whether to charge more on the apps than at the counter.
mechanics.engineMath: Revenue is recorded by channel. For each channel: contribution = sales x (1 - 0.28 cost of goods - channelTakes) - packaging. channelTakes comes from extra.channels: counter 4.1%, own order-ahead 6.8%, app pickup 9%, basic delivery 23%, promoted delivery up to 43%, catering marketplace 18%. Delivery tickets are larger (two drinks, a pastry) and the player may set an app price up to 15% above the counter price, which most restaurants do; a higher app price lowers app orders with the same elasticity. Delivery and order-ahead load the bar in the rush like any other order (hourly_peak) but need no seat. The city's caps bound what an app may take; an 'enhanced' plan is the player's choice, never a default. This replaces the fixed monthly costs used as a stand-in by the delivery_apps, order_ahead and catering levers.

mechanics.title: A rival opening or closing is announced, and it is not the end
mechanics.playerDecision: What to change in the month between the announcement and the opening: entry price, loyalty, beans, hours, a seasonal drink.
mechanics.engineMath: Chains and carts are non-playing rivals placed by the city deck on real vacant doors, announced a month ahead. A rival carries a type (chain, discount app chain, small-format chain, cart), a price index (chain 0.9, discount 0.6 during its opening quarter, cart 0.5) and the segments it pulls (commuters and students first, regulars last). In the footfall model it joins the split of passers-by with its own weight: 1.0 for a chain in its first six months (curiosity plus opening offers), 0.5 afterwards (the keen-cray staticWeight). The hit on a player's shop is larger the more its quality and price resemble the rival's: a differentiated shop (quality above 0.6) loses about a third as much. When a rival closes, its share is released over two months and split by attractiveness; a shop at capacity gets nothing. Planning size: -7% for six months when a chain opens within 250 m, +6% when one closes.

mechanics.title: Regulars are built slowly and lost one disappointment at a time
mechanics.playerDecision: Whether to spend on getting first visits (opening offer, listings, a seasonal drink) or on second visits (loyalty, the same barista, speed).
mechanics.engineMath: Split each segment's customers into regulars and newcomers. Regulars: a stock that grows each month by newcomers x conversion and shrinks by churn. Conversion from first visit to regular: 30% at average quality (range 20-45% with quality and loyalty); churn of regulars: 4% a month at rest, +10 points in a month with slow_service_reviews, +5 after price_step_backlash, +15 when a shift lead or senior barista leaves (task D05). Regulars buy 2-4 times a week and bring a newcomer now and then (0.05 a month each). Newcomers are driven by footfall, the map rating and the letter grade; regulars by none of those. This is the engine's 'awareness' ramp with a cause: a new shop starts with no regulars, which is why month one sells a third of month six; and a bought shop keeps the regulars only while it keeps what they came for. At steady state regulars should give 55-65% of orders.

mechanics.title: Customers remember last month's price
mechanics.playerDecision: How fast to raise prices: in one jump or in small steps, and whether to keep one cheap item on the board.
mechanics.engineMath: The engine's reference price is fixed at $8.50. Make it move: fairPrice rises 4% a year with the street (menu_prices_drift_up). Each shop also has a remembered price: last month's price for its regulars. A rise of up to 4% within a month costs only the ordinary elasticity; above that, regulars churn faster (price_step_backlash: 3% of demand for two months, a quarter-star less in that month's reviews). A cut is noticed slower than a rise: half the elasticity in the first month. A value item (value_anchor) lowers the price sensitivity of students and commuters by a third because the board shows a number they accept. A card surcharge counts as a price rise of its size for card payers.

mechanics.title: A monthly pass: cash up front, margin at the mercy of the heaviest users
mechanics.playerDecision: Whether to sell a pass, at what price, and with what cap.
mechanics.engineMath: A pass is sold to regulars: price P a month for up to C drip coffees. Take-up: 5% of regulars at P = $45, C = 30, falling with price. A holder drinks min(C, 22) cups a month on average instead of 12, and buys food on one visit in four. Shop's month per holder: +P cash on day one, -cups x $0.80 ingredients and cup, +extra food margin; the list-price sales they would have made anyway (12 x $3.75 = $45) are gone. So a $45 pass with a 30-cup cap is roughly neutral on coffee and earns on food and on the habit; an uncapped pass loses on the top tenth of users. The cash arrives before the coffee is poured, which helps a thin month and is a liability on the books.

nonObvious.text: A cafe runs out of bar, not out of customers: at 200 orders a day the 8am hour alone brings 28 to 36 orders, and one barista makes about 25.
nonObvious.why: Monthly capacity looks fine on paper while the shop turns people away every morning and stands idle every afternoon. The fix is the schedule, not headcount.

nonObvious.text: More than half of a coffee chain's day is over by 11am.
nonObvious.why: Starbucks makes over half its US store sales before 11am; a commuter shop is nearer 53% and a neighborhood shop about 46%. The afternoon crew costs the same per hour and sells half as much.

nonObvious.text: People judge a line by how long it looks, not by how fast it moves.
nonObvious.why: A fast bar with eight people in the doorway loses more walk-ins than a slow one with three. Where the line stands and how it is seen from the street matter as much as speed.

nonObvious.text: Phone orders can lose you walk-in customers.
nonObvious.why: When a fifth of rush orders came by phone, Starbucks found people saw the crowd at the handoff and left without ordering. Order-ahead needs a cap in the rush.

nonObvious.text: A star on Yelp is worth 5-9% of revenue to an independent and nothing to a chain.
nonObvious.why: People already know what a chain is. Reviews are how a stranger decides about you, so they matter most on tourist streets and least among regulars.

nonObvious.text: A 4.24 and a 4.26 are the same cafe, but one shows four stars and the other four and a half.
nonObvious.why: Ratings are rounded to half stars, and the jump at the rounding line changed how often restaurants sold out by 19 percentage points.

nonObvious.text: A quarter of your Yelp reviews may never count, and the ones you asked for are the first to go.
nonObvious.why: Yelp says about 75% of reviews are 'recommended'; the rest are hidden from the rating. Reviews from first-time reviewers and solicited reviews are filtered most.

nonObvious.text: A free cookie for a five-star review is a federal violation.
nonObvious.why: The FTC's 2024 review rule bans rewards that depend on what the review says, with penalties up to $53,088 per violation. Asking everyone for an honest review is legal.

nonObvious.text: Answering reviews raises the rating.
nonObvious.why: Hotels that began replying gained 0.12 stars, and a third of them moved up a displayed half star within six months. Future reviewers write more carefully when they see the owner reads.

nonObvious.text: With a B at re-inspection you may post 'Grade Pending' and argue your case; you may not leave the window empty.
nonObvious.why: The pending card is legal until the hearing and reads better than a B. A missing card is a separate fine and an easy 311 complaint for a neighbor.

nonObvious.text: An office-district cafe earns its week in three days.
nonObvious.why: Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday hold 70% of weekday office visits; Friday holds 12%, and 11.9% in New York. Rent is paid for seven days.

nonObvious.text: For a neighborhood cafe Saturday is the best day and Monday the worst.
nonObvious.why: Cafes and bakeries sell 15% above their weekly average on Saturday and about 10% below it on Monday: the opposite of an office block. The same staffing plan cannot serve both.

nonObvious.text: The city's weekends recovered; its weekdays did not.
nonObvious.why: Weekend subway ridership is at 89% of 2019, weekday ridership at 74%. A lease priced on pre-pandemic weekday crowds is priced on people who are not there.

nonObvious.text: August is the national peak for eating out and a slow month in New York.
nonObvious.why: Residents leave, offices thin out from late July to Labor Day and students are gone. Tourist streets are the exception.

nonObvious.text: The worst office weeks are not in summer: they run from Thanksgiving into January.
nonObvious.why: Office visits in December 2025 were 33% under 2019, against 22% under in July. A commuter-fed cafe should plan its cash for a weak December and January, not only for August.

nonObvious.text: A delivery app's 15% is not the whole bill.
nonObvious.why: New York caps delivery at 15%, basic service at 5% and card processing at 3%: 23% together. Since 2025 an app may sell 'enhanced' services for up to 20% more. On a small coffee ticket the promoted plan leaves under 30 cents of contribution per dollar.

nonObvious.text: If an app overcharged you, the city can get the money back.
nonObvious.why: In April 2026 the consumer agency won more than $580,000 in refunds for over 380 restaurants from one delivery app that broke the fee caps.

nonObvious.text: Higher courier pay did not shrink delivery in New York.
nonObvious.why: The city forecast fewer orders when it set the courier minimum. Orders rose instead: 3.3 million a week in mid-2026, 700,000 more than in December 2023.

nonObvious.text: You cannot add a card fee at the register, but you can post two prices.
nonObvious.why: State law requires the posted price to be the full credit card price, and the city bars restaurants from adding surcharge lines. A cash price next to a card price is the lawful form, and it still costs customers: most people switch payment or shop to avoid it.

nonObvious.text: A chain opening next door hurts the afternoon more than the morning, and it can be answered.
nonObvious.why: One owner lost a tenth of afternoon sales to a new Starbucks and won them back by adding breakfast sandwiches. Between near-identical stores the measured effect is about 1% per neighbor.

nonObvious.text: Chains are leaving New York faster than they arrive.
nonObvious.why: Chain stores fell in six of the last eight years; Starbucks closed 42 city stores in 2025. Each closure releases a few hundred daily customers to whoever is nearest and fast enough.

nonObvious.text: The new rival is not Starbucks: it is an app with $1.99 coffee and a 500-square-foot counter.
nonObvious.why: An app-first chain went from 2 to 22 New York stores in about a year, and a small-format chain with automatic machines reached 106 stores. Both sell the commuter's cup cheaper than a full cafe can.

nonObvious.text: The city is licensing thousands more food carts, and a coffee cart needs no rent.
nonObvious.why: 2,200 more vendor licenses a year from 2026 to 2031. A cart at the subway stairs sells coffee for about $2, where your commuters pass first.

nonObvious.text: Regulars are a few hundred people who pay most of the rent.
nonObvious.why: A regular brings six times the yearly revenue of a one-time customer; at one roastery two thirds of revenue came from repeat customers. Losing one barista they like can cost more than a bad review.

nonObvious.text: Most first-time customers do not come back.
nonObvious.why: Between a fifth and two thirds of first visitors are gone within 100 days. The opening crowd is not the customer base; the second visit is what must be earned.

nonObvious.text: Closing at 3pm can be the right decision.
nonObvious.why: The last four hours carry about a quarter of a neighborhood cafe's orders and a full crew's wages. Below about 100 orders a day the afternoon loses money.

nonObvious.text: An 'unlimited' coffee pass will be capped sooner or later.
nonObvious.why: The best-known subscription ran four years as unlimited and then limited holders to 30 drinks a month: the heaviest users drink the margin.

nonObvious.text: A dog-friendly cafe is illegal indoors in New York.
nonObvious.why: Only service dogs may enter a food establishment; pet dogs are allowed in outdoor seating with a posted sign. A dog inside is a Health Department violation and counts toward the letter grade.

nonObvious.text: Flyers are fined per flyer.
nonObvious.why: Each one taped to a pole or tucked under a wiper is a separate violation of $75 to $250, and the fine goes to the business named on it. Handing flyers to people is legal.

nonObvious.text: Prices on the street rise about 4% a year, so standing still is a price cut.
nonObvious.why: Median drip coffee rose 4.3% and cold brew 4.0% in a year. Customers accept small regular steps; they notice a jump.

nonObvious.text: When the chain down the street closed its restrooms to non-customers, the requests moved to its neighbors.
nonObvious.why: Starbucks ended its open-door policy in January 2025. A cafe with fewer than 20 seats has no duty to offer a restroom at all, and saying yes has a cleaning cost.

nonObvious.text: Taste, not price, is what people say makes them pick one coffee shop over another.
nonObvious.why: In a 2025 survey of 650 coffee drinkers 53% named taste, 20% price, 17% convenience and 8% atmosphere. What they say and what they do differ, but it is a reason not to compete on price alone.

nonObvious.text: Going viral is a capacity problem.
nonObvious.why: A Brooklyn cafe had to cut its line off at 3pm; a Manhattan luncheonette had two-to-three-hour waits for months and 'wasn't ready'. The surge leaves reviews behind, good or bad, long after the crowd is gone.

nonObvious.text: In New York a coffee cart charges about $2, a chain about $3 and a specialty bar $6 to $8 for a milk drink.
nonObvious.why: Three price worlds share one sidewalk. A cafe that prices like a specialty bar and serves like a chain is compared with the cheaper one.

nonObvious.text: Evenings belong to a different kind of cafe.
nonObvious.why: Late-night coffee is growing where coffee, not alcohol, is the social drink: Yemeni-style cafes stay open late across North America, and some New York shops turn into wine or sake bars after dark. An ordinary espresso bar that simply stays open later rarely covers the payroll.

nonObvious.text: The average cafe is rated about 4.3, so 4.0 is below average.
nonObvious.why: A sample of 500 US cafe profiles averaged 4.26 stars and 15% of restaurants sat under 4.0. Two in three customers filter at four stars, so 'four stars' is the floor, not a good score.

nonObvious.text: Taking the grade card down hides very little.
nonObvious.why: Review sites have shown New York inspection results on restaurant pages since 2013, and the city publishes every inspection. The card in the window is only the most visible copy.

nonObvious.text: Four in ten hybrid workers come to the office for a coffee and leave.
nonObvious.why: 'Coffee badging' was 58% of hybrid workers in 2023 and 43% in 2025. The office crowd an owner counts at 8:30 is thinner by lunch, which is why office-district cafes sell more than half their day before 11am.

nonObvious.text: Your reviews can disappear through no fault of yours.
nonObvious.why: Display faults at the largest map platform hid reviews for weeks in February and October 2025; one business dropped from about 600 reviews to 460 before they came back. A shop with 40 reviews feels that; a shop with 800 does not.
